strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: selecting compatible pretrained vision encoders and language models without fully training every combination. Jointly reducing the search space and evaluation cost is a sensible approach.
The exhaustive search provides a useful reference. Across six benchmarks, Mordal reportedly recovers the best candidate on five tasks while reducing training GPU hours by 8.9–11.6×.

The paper includes component ablations, a runtime breakdown, and hyperparameter sensitivity experiments. These provide preliminary evidence that clustering, early stopping, and performance extrapolation each contribute to efficiency.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is insufficient to establish competitiveness. Exhaustive grid search is expensive by construction; comparisons against budget-matched random search, successive halving or Hyperband over the full candidate pool, and learning-curve extrapolation without clustering are missing. The ablations retain clustering and therefore do not isolate its advantage over standard resource-allocation methods. The methodological novelty largely consists of combining established techniques.

The scaling predictor contains consequential inconsistencies. Algorithm 1 fits log(error) against log(r), but evaluates f(1) for full-data performance, whose correct input is log(1)=0. It also stops when fitting loss exceeds the threshold, whereas the prose describes stopping once a satisfactory log-linear relationship is found; no explicit fallback or minimum sample ratio is given. These may be presentation errors, but they leave the implemented selection rule unclear.

The scaling-law justification is weak. Fixing model size in Equation 3 leaves an additive constant, so log(loss) is not generally linear in log(data), and downstream task error is not the cross-entropy loss in that equation. Figure 9 shows selected curves for one language model on two tasks, without quantitative full-data prediction errors, uncertainty, or validation across the remaining language models and tasks. Reliable extrapolation from small data fractions is central to the method and needs stronger evidence.

The clustering assumptions are inadequately validated. CKA is not generally invariant to arbitrary MLP transformations, contrary to the justification in Section 3.1. The supporting experiment uses representations from trained projection heads, whereas search depends on representations available before full alignment. Evidence is limited to four vision encoders with one fixed language model; there is no comparable validation of language-model clustering or of medoid performance as a reliable proxy for an entire cluster.

The evaluation protocol does not clearly distinguish the labeled data used repeatedly for candidate selection and extrapolation from an independent held-out test set. Consequently, the reader cannot establish whether reported gains generalize beyond the selection data. Repeated runs, confidence intervals, and variability in candidate recovery are also absent despite random data sampling and stochastic training.

Reproducibility and compute accounting need clarification. Table 4 lists eight vision encoders and eight language models, conflicting with the stated seven-by-seven, 49-candidate search. Important details such as LoRA configuration, training duration, exact evaluation splits, and clustering linkage are missing. The runtime breakdown covers early stopping and scaling prediction but does not establish whether representation extraction, projector warmup, clustering, benchmark evaluation, and final selected-model training are included in the headline savings.

The claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Experiments use one alignment dataset, one main architecture and training recipe, and roughly 7B language models. ChartQA selection reaches 18.6 versus the grid-search optimum of 20.2, qualifying claims of finding the best model. The abstract's claim of outperforming state-of-the-art counterparts is not supported by matched comparisons: the principal accuracy reference is a retrained LLaVA-1.5-style configuration, rather than the stronger VLMs highlighted in the introduction.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: selecting compatible pretrained vision encoders and language models without fully training every combination.

The evaluation includes an exhaustive reference over 49 combinations and six benchmarks. Mordal recovers the best candidate on five benchmarks, with reported GPU-hour savings of 8.9×–11.6× relative to exhaustive search.

The framework combines representation-based clustering, successive halving, and performance extrapolation into a coherent workflow. Component ablations and a limited hyperparameter sensitivity study provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The competitive evaluation is insufficient. Exhaustive search is the only external search baseline; there are no budget-matched comparisons with random search, standalone successive halving/Hyperband, or established multi-fidelity optimization methods. The ablations retain substantial parts of Mordal and do not establish its advantage over simpler alternatives. Consequently, the headline speedup does not demonstrate a competitive accuracy–compute tradeoff.

The scaling-prediction mechanism has unresolved mathematical and algorithmic issues. Fixing N in Equation 3 leaves an additive constant, so log(loss) is not generally linear in log(D); applying this relationship to downstream error requires separate justification. Algorithm 1 fits log(error) against log(r) but evaluates f_c(1), whereas full-data prediction corresponds to log(1)=0. It also stops when fitting loss exceeds the threshold, conflicting with the prose about detecting a good fit, and provides no explicit termination bound. These may be presentation errors, but they directly affect reproducibility of a central component.

Evidence for reliable extrapolation is limited to qualitative curves for five encoders with one language model on two tasks. Figure 9 plots error against log sample count rather than directly validating the claimed log–log relationship. There are no held-out extrapolation errors, prediction intervals, or systematic tests of ranking accuracy across different language models and tasks.

The evaluation protocol does not clearly separate task data used for adaptive selection from held-out data used for final reporting. Dataset splits, selection-set sizes, and safeguards against repeatedly selecting on the reported benchmark are unspecified. No repeated search runs, seed variation, or uncertainty estimates are reported, leaving the reliability of winner recovery unclear.

The clustering premise is weakly validated. The supporting experiment covers only four vision encoders, one language model, and two tasks, without directly validating conditional language-model clustering. In ScienceQA, CLIP and DFN have CKA similarity 0.86 but differ by 5.3 accuracy points in Table 3. The claim that MLP projection preserves CKA properties is not generally justified. The paper also acknowledges that cluster elimination discards strong candidates, but does not quantify this risk systematically.

The novelty and significance claims exceed the evidence. The main techniques are established, and the contribution is primarily their integration for VLM component selection. The abstract's claim of outperforming state-of-the-art counterparts is not supported by the main comparison against a LLaVA-1.5-equivalent configuration. Evaluation uses one alignment dataset and approximately 7B language models; moreover, Mordal misses the ChartQA winner, obtaining 18.6 versus 20.2, which limits unconditional claims of finding the best VLM.

Important implementation and reporting details remain unclear, including LoRA configuration, training duration, projector warmup, and whether reported search costs include clustering, validation, and final training. Results also contain unexplained discrepancies: CLIP–Vicuna's ScienceQA score is 70.4 in Table 1 but 67.6 in Table 3. The ranking metric alternates between ordinary and weighted Kendall correlation, without adequately specifying weights or treatment of candidates eliminated together.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: selecting compatible pretrained vision encoders and language models without exhaustively aligning every combination.
The combination of representation-based clustering, successive halving, and learning-curve extrapolation forms a coherent search pipeline.
The evaluation includes 49 model combinations and six downstream benchmarks. Mordal recovers the grid-search optimum on five benchmarks while reporting 8.9–11.6× lower GPU costs.
Component ablations and hyperparameter sensitivity experiments provide useful evidence about the efficiency–ranking tradeoff.
weaknesses: The central efficiency comparison is insufficiently competitive. Grid search is the only main baseline; there are no compute-matched comparisons against random search, standalone successive halving/Hyperband, or established learning-curve search methods. The ablations retain clustering and therefore do not establish its advantage over simpler resource-allocation strategies. Since the components are largely established techniques, these comparisons are particularly important for demonstrating a meaningful contribution.

The scaling predictor has unresolved mathematical and algorithmic issues. Equation 3 includes an additive constant, so fixing model size does not imply a linear relationship between log(error) and log(data). Algorithm 1 fits on log(r) but predicts full-data performance using f(1), although full data corresponds to log(1)=0. It also stops when fitting loss exceeds the threshold, contrary to the accompanying description of accepting a good fit. These may be presentation errors, but the implemented procedure and its validity are unclear.

Evidence for extrapolation accuracy is limited. Figure 9 covers only two tasks with a fixed Qwen2 backbone and provides neither quantitative prediction errors nor uncertainty estimates. Demonstrating approximate trends does not establish reliable extrapolation from small subsets to full-data performance, especially when learning curves cross.

The evaluation protocol does not clearly distinguish the target-task data used for repeated selection from an independent held-out test set. It also reports no repeated search runs or confidence intervals despite random data subsampling and training variability. Consequently, selection robustness and unbiased downstream generalization remain unestablished.

The clustering justification is weakly validated. Section 4.3 examines four vision encoders with one language model, using representations after projector training, whereas search relies on representations available before full alignment. It does not directly validate language-model clustering or quantify the risk of discarding strong candidates. The assertion that MLP projection preserves the relevant CKA properties is also not generally justified.

Claims exceed the demonstrated scope. The abstract claims newly discovered VLMs outperform state-of-the-art counterparts, but the main comparison is against a LLaVA-1.5-equivalent configuration rather than the stronger contemporary models displayed in Figure 1. Experiments use one alignment dataset and approximately 7B language models. On ChartQA, Mordal obtains 18.6 versus the optimum of 20.2, so claims of consistently finding the best candidate need qualification.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. Important details such as LoRA configuration, precise evaluation splits, clustering linkage, and complete search-cost accounting are unclear. Hyperparameter defaults differ between the interface example and appendix; ScienceQA results differ between Tables 1 and 3 without explanation. The ranking metric also shifts between ordinary and weighted Kendall correlation and between all candidates and the oracle top ten.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: selecting compatible pretrained vision encoders and language models under limited alignment compute. Task-dependent performance differences provide a convincing motivation.

The combination of representation-based clustering, successive halving, and performance extrapolation is a sensible engineering approach. Reported results recover the grid-search winner on six of seven benchmarks while reducing GPU hours by 8.9–11.6×.

The evaluation includes multiple vision and language backbones, component ablations, runtime breakdowns, and additional small-model experiments. The appendix also accounts explicitly for clustering and projector warmup costs.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish competitiveness against the most relevant alternatives. Grid search and transferability metrics are insufficient for evaluating an adaptive training-based search method. Missing baselines include successive halving or Hyperband over the entire candidate pool, uniform partial training ranked directly by task accuracy, and learning-curve extrapolation without clustering. The ablations retain clustering and therefore do not isolate its value against straightforward budget-matched search. Since the main ingredients are established techniques, this is a substantial gap in both novelty and empirical justification.

The scaling predictor is not specified consistently enough to establish technical soundness. Algorithm 1 fits log(error) against log(r), but returns f_c(1); full-data prediction requires evaluation at log(1)=0, followed by exponentiation to recover error. It stops when fitting loss exceeds the threshold, contrary to the prose about detecting a satisfactory fit, without specifying whether the violating point is discarded or providing a termination safeguard. Reusing intermediate checkpoints also needs justification under the stated data-size-dependent linear learning-rate schedule.

Evidence for reliable extrapolation is limited to qualitative curves for two tasks with one language backbone. There are no held-out full-data prediction errors, uncertainty estimates, or systematic analyses of ranking reversals. Equation 3's additive loss floor does not generally yield a linear relationship between log(error) and log(data), so the proposed extrapolation requires stronger empirical validation.

The evaluation protocol does not clearly separate target-task data used repeatedly for search and hyperparameter selection from an untouched final test set. Seeds, repeated searches, and confidence intervals are absent despite stochastic training, sampling, and potentially irreversible pruning decisions. Consequently, the reliability of the reported winner recovery and ranking improvements is unclear.

The justification for clustering is weaker than claimed. CKA is not generally invariant to an arbitrary learned MLP projection, and high representation similarity does not guarantee similar downstream accuracy or preserve the best candidate within a cluster. The small illustrative examples do not quantify within-cluster performance spread or the frequency with which medoid-based pruning discards strong candidates.

Appendix D.4 presents an unresolved comparison problem: removing projector warmup does not remove the training used by Mordal's early stopping and scaling prediction. If that training remains, comparison with genuinely training-free baselines is not under the stated constraint. If it is removed, the paper does not explain how representation similarity alone produces an absolute performance ranking.

Reproducibility and claim precision need improvement. Table 6 lists eight language models although the experiments repeatedly specify seven and 49 combinations, leaving the actual search pool ambiguous. Important training details, including LoRA configuration and training duration, are missing, and the advertised code link is blank. Claims of finding the best model should consistently acknowledge the ChartQA failure: Mordal achieves 18.6 versus the grid-search optimum of 20.2. These issues, together with the missing search baselines and predictor ambiguities, leave the contribution below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: selecting compatible vision encoders and language models without fully training every combination. Jointly reducing the candidate pool and evaluation cost is a sensible approach.

The reported results are promising: Mordal recovers the grid-search winner on six of seven main benchmarks while reducing GPU hours by 8.9–11.6×. Its weighted Kendall correlation exceeds the four transferability baselines across all seven tasks.

The evaluation includes component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, computational breakdowns, and additional experiments with smaller language models. These provide useful evidence beyond a single benchmark or configuration.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish competitiveness against strong budgeted search methods. The method combines established CKA clustering, successive halving, and learning-curve extrapolation, but lacks matched-budget comparisons with standalone successive halving/Hyperband, random search, or direct ranking by partially trained task performance. The transferability baselines receive partial-training budgets, yet are ranked through surrogate metrics rather than their actual downstream scores. Consequently, the benefit of Mordal's particular combination over simpler alternatives remains unclear.

The scaling predictor is technically inconsistent as specified. Algorithm 1 fits log(error) against log(r), but returns f_c(1); full-data evaluation corresponds to log(1)=0, with exponentiation needed to recover error. It also terminates when fitting loss exceeds the threshold and returns that fit, contrary to the stated goal of detecting reliable log-linearity. There is no explicit termination safeguard when the fit remains good. These may be presentation errors, but they affect the central algorithm and require correction and implementation verification.

Evidence for reliable extrapolation is insufficient. Equation 3 contains an additive error floor, so fixing model size does not generally yield a linear relationship between log(error) and log(data). Figure 7 presents raw error against log sample count for only two tasks and one language backbone, without held-out extrapolation errors or uncertainty. Reusing intermediate checkpoints also requires explaining how their learning-rate schedules and data exposure correspond to separately trained smaller-data models.

The evaluation protocol does not clearly distinguish the target-task data used repeatedly for pruning, extrapolation, and hyperparameter selection from an untouched final test set. This prevents assessing selection overfitting. No repeated-search statistics, seed variation, confidence intervals, or budget-versus-regret curves are reported, despite stochastic sampling and irreversible pruning decisions.

The justification for clustering is weaker than claimed. CKA similarity does not guarantee similar task accuracy, and CKA is not generally invariant to arbitrary learned MLP transformations, contrary to the justification in Section 3.1. The motivating examples are small, and the paper lacks a systematic analysis of within-cluster performance dispersion, discarded winners, or comparison with random clustering and a complete no-clustering search baseline.

Several inconsistencies undermine reproducibility. Table 6 lists eight LLMs despite the stated seven-LLM, 49-candidate search space. The scaling threshold differs between Listing 1 and Appendix D, and important LoRA and training details are missing. Appendix D.4 describes a training-free Mordal variant but does not explain how similarity alone produces quality rankings or replaces its training-dependent evaluation stages. The code-availability footnote is empty, while the reproducibility statement promises a future release.

Some conclusions exceed the evidence. Table 2 misses the ChartQA winner, obtaining 18.6 versus 20.2, despite broader claims of retaining top-1 performance. Appendix A claims the best model remains unchanged after task-specific fine-tuning, but ChartQA switches from CLIP–Vicuna in Table 1 to SigLIP–Vicuna in Table 5. The small Q-former study evaluates similarity rather than end-to-end search effectiveness. Overall, the promising efficiency results do not yet outweigh the unresolved algorithmic and evaluation issues at a top-tier conference.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: selecting compatible pretrained vision encoders and language models without exhaustively training every combination. Task-dependent differences in component quality provide a convincing motivation.

The reported results are promising: Mordal recovers the grid-search winner on six of seven benchmarks while reducing GPU hours by 8.9–11.6×, and consistently improves weighted Kendall correlation over the evaluated transferability methods.

The framework combines representation clustering, successive halving, and performance extrapolation coherently. Component ablations, computational breakdowns, and additional small-model experiments provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish competitiveness against strong budgeted search methods. Grid search is expensive by construction, while EMMS, LogME, LEEP, and NLEEP are primarily transferability estimators. Missing comparisons include successive halving or Hyperband over the complete candidate pool, uniform partial training ranked by downstream performance, and learning-curve extrapolation without clustering. Since the components are established techniques, these comparisons are essential to demonstrate the integration's added value.

The scaling predictor has unresolved technical inconsistencies. Algorithm 1 fits log(error) against log(r) but returns f_c(1), whereas full-data prediction corresponds to log(1)=0. It also stops when fitting loss exceeds the threshold and returns that fit, without explaining whether the offending point is discarded or providing a termination safeguard. Equation 3 includes an additive error floor and therefore does not directly imply the fitted log-linear relationship. Figure 7 offers qualitative curves for only two tasks with one LLM, without quantitative held-out extrapolation errors.

The evaluation protocol does not clearly distinguish target-task data used repeatedly for selection from an independent final test set. Consequently, it is difficult to assess selection-induced optimism. No repeated-search results, seed variation, or confidence intervals are reported, despite stochastic sampling and potentially irreversible pruning decisions.

The clustering assumption is insufficiently validated. CKA similarity does not generally guarantee similar downstream accuracy, and CKA is not invariant to arbitrary MLP transformations as the justification in Section 3.1 appears to suggest. The paper lacks a systematic analysis relating similarity to performance differences across the full candidate pool, or a direct comparison against search without clustering.

Appendix D.4's training-free comparison is internally unclear. Removing projector warmup does not remove the alignment training used by Mordal's early stopping and scaling prediction. If these stages remain, the comparison is not training-free; if they are replaced by similarity-only evaluation, the paper does not specify how similarity produces an absolute quality ranking.

Reproducibility and claim precision need improvement. Table 6 lists eight LLMs despite the stated seven-LLM, 49-candidate search; key LoRA and training details are missing; and source code is promised rather than supplied. The blanket best-model claims also overlook ChartQA, where Mordal selects a model scoring 18.6 versus the optimum of 20.2. These issues, together with the missing search baselines, prevent the promising results from supporting acceptance at the stated standard.
